title: The other summit season: BRICS and the SCO have spotted a gap
author: Nick Bisley
text: |BRICS, explained.Australia's neighbours are positioning themselves as the broader global order changes (Getty Images)The other summit season: BRICS and the SCO have spotted a gapAs authoritarian states find common cause in reforming global institutions, Australia must reckon with a changing neighbourhood.Nick Bisley24 September 20264 min read|The other summit season: BRICS and the SCO have spotted a gapThe other summit season: BRICS and the SCO have spotted a gapNovember is normally Asia’s multilateral “summit season”.In the early part of the millennium, the region was gripped by enthusiasm for building institutional mechanisms. This created something of a scheduling conundrum. How could summit meetings be held in a way that gave each new institution enough oxygen while not condemning leaders to be forever in the departure lounge? The answer: Asia’s summit season. ASEAN, APEC, the East Asia Summit and then various ASEAN Plus Ones are normally all held in quick succession. Occasionally, when the stars align, a G20 meeting is arranged as well.This month, the world has had a taste of a new and different summit season in Asia as the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s 26th meeting fell two weeks prior to the BRICS summit. While not quite as cheek-by-jowl as Asia’s summits, the proximity of the two groupings, along with their growing prominence and influence, warrants reflection, especially as each has become a focal point for cooperation among illiberal and authoritarian states.The SCO and BRICS were once niche areas of interest. For the acronymically enthusiastic international relations scholar, knowing what they were and who belonged to each was something of a badge of pride. Today, both SCO and BRICS meetings garner global headlines. This attention is in part due to the membership and reach of the groups. The SCO comprises ten members including Russia, China, Iran and India, with another 17 observer and partner states including Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Cambodia and Egypt. It is one of few international groupings that recognises Myanmar’s junta government and also attracts the ASEAN Secretariat and the UN as regular participants.The recent expansion of the groupings is part of a larger trend in which illiberal and authoritarian powers are increasingly cooperating to advance their interests. BRICS is a bigger affair and has global reach. Beyond the original five (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), its members include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Indonesia and the UAE. Representing half the world’s population and 40% of global GDP, the body has critical mass.The SCO is more than a quarter-century old while BRICS is a post-GFC creation founded in 2009. Yet for much of their existence, beyond some rhetorical flourishes, their ambitions were relatively limited. The SCO was for its first dozen years or so focused primarily on Central Asian border security and counter-terrorism. While BRICS sought major reforms of the global economic order, it had to settle for the creation of a relatively meagre new development bank in 2014.Both groupings have, in recent years, sought to position themselves in more expansive terms. This has come in part through the admission of new members. The SCO’s membership expanded from 2017 while new members joined BRICS from 2023 onwards. With the larger geographic footprint has come expanded ambition.Here, the two bodies differ. The SCO, which timed its 25th summit last year to coincide with China’s Second World War commemorations, is geopolitically ambitious but ultimately focused on security matters in Central Asia and Eurasia. While it has issued broad-ranging statements about international order and globalisation, there has been little of substance beyond grand rhetoric.BRICS is far more ambitious. At its most recent summit, the New Delhi Declaration ran to nearly 45 pages, covering everything from UN reform to restructuring of the Bretton Woods Institutions, people-to-people diplomacy and even new university ranking systems. If the SCO is ultimately about security, BRICS wants to restructure international order along lines it considers more representative of the world, and of the Global South.The recent expansion of the groupings is part of a larger trend in which illiberal and authoritarian powers are increasingly cooperating to advance their interests. They are doing so not just because of the ambitions and growing power of their members but because they sense an opportunity created by the failings of existing institutions. The criticisms of the institutions built by the old North Atlantic world – that they are unrepresentative of contemporary realities, that they do not serve the needs of the world’s less well-off, that they are dysfunctional or worse – are real. BRICS and the SCO have spotted a gap in the institutional market. The West has been slow to notice.For Australia, a further development is of note. Both BRICS and the SCO were once groupings of little interest to Southeast Asian states. In recent years, this has begun to change. Indonesia’s interest in BRICS is telling; Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam all took part in the 2026 summit alongside the ASEAN chair. Myanmar and Laos have become dialogue partners of the SCO, and ASEAN has been represented at recent summits.This in part reflects the widening reach of these groupings and their efforts to advance less Western-centred forms of cooperation. It also reflects a trend of Southeast Asian states looking beyond ASEAN for influence and advantage. This move is not necessarily something that will cost ASEAN, but from an Australian point of view, it is crucial to understand the ways its neighbours are positioning themselves as the broader global order changes.About the authorNick BisleyNick Bisley is Pro Vice-Chancellor Research and Professor of International Relations at La Trobe University.TopicsBRICSASEANSoutheast AsiaDiplomacyAustraliaThe Interpreter on BRICSExplore The InterpreterSoutheast AsiaIndia’s role in Southeast Asia’s BRICS bet18 September 2026Yanitha Meena LouisBRICSBRICS reaches for a crescendo17 September 2026Stacy JarvisBRICSBRICS grits its teeth through a New Delhi breakthrough14 September 2026Aarti BetigeriMore on BRICSExplore BRICSResearchThe rise of authoritarian cooperation: A new illiberal order?Analysis by Nick Bisley
